name: Snapper
description: A pink and silver fish with blue speckles, a steep forehead and a strong spiny dorsal fin.
funFact: A large snapper can be older than 60 years.
clue: Bays, harbours and coastal reefs, particularly in northern waters.
aliases: New Zealand snapper, Australasian snapper, Pink snapper, pannie (a pan-sized snapper), moocher (a big snapper), Tāmure, Karatī (young snapper), Pepe tāmure (snapper fry)

name: Kahawai
description: A fast schooling fish with a green-blue back, silver flanks and dark markings along its upper sides.
funFact: Young kahawai can reach roughly 15 cm during their first year.
clue: Surf beaches, river mouths and feeding schools around the coast.
aliases: Australian salmon, Eastern Australian salmon, Sea trout, Sea salmon, KY, Kōhere (young kahawai), Kōwaitau (young kahawai), Koria (kahawai fry)

name: Yellowtail kingfish
description: A muscular, streamlined fish with a golden side stripe and a vivid yellow forked tail.
funFact: New Zealand fish dominate the international angling record list for yellowtail kingfish.
clue: Reefs, headlands and offshore baitfish schools.
aliases: Yellowtail kingfish, Yellowtail, Yellowtail amberjack, kingi, rat (a small kingfish), Haku, Makumaku, Warehenga
imageCredit: Image: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · Public domain

creditLinks.text: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Blue cod
description: A bottom-dwelling New Zealand native with a rounded head, fleshy lips and blue-grey adult colouring.
funFact: Some blue cod change from female to male as they grow.
clue: Rocky seabeds and reef edges, especially south of Cook Strait.
aliases: New Zealand blue cod, Rock cod, Rāwaru, Pākirikiri (also used for the spotty), Taipua, Kopukopu, Pātutuki

name: Tarakihi
description: A silver schooling fish distinguished by a black shoulder saddle and an extended pectoral fin ray.
funFact: Tarakihi can survive for more than four decades.
clue: Coastal shelf waters and deeper reef margins.
aliases: Jackass morwong (Australia), Morwong, terakihi (common misspelling), teraki (common misspelling)

name: Trevally
description: A deep silver fish with a yellowish tail, blue-green back and a dark mark on the gill cover.
funFact: Seagrass meadows provide important nursery habitat for young trevally.
clue: Northern coastal reefs, harbours and sandy channels.
aliases: Silver trevally, trev, Araara, Raumarie, Raumarire

name: Red gurnard
description: A red seabed hunter with an armoured head and broad pectoral fins patterned in blue and green.
funFact: Muscles around its swim bladder produce several kinds of grunts and growls.
clue: Sandy and muddy coastal bottoms.
aliases: Gurnard, Bluefin gurnard, grunter, Kumukumu, Pūwhaiau

name: John dory
description: An extremely thin, deep-bodied ambush hunter with long dorsal spines and a dark circular flank spot.
funFact: Viewed from the front, its narrow body almost vanishes.
clue: Weedy bays and reef edges, particularly in northern waters.
aliases: Dory, jon dory, jon dore, JD, Kuparu, Pukeru

name: Blue moki
description: A deep blue-grey fish with a small thick-lipped mouth and no elongated pectoral ray.
funFact: Some blue moki have been aged at more than 40 years.
clue: Rocky coasts and neighbouring sand, mainly from the Bay of Plenty south.
aliases: Moki, Moki

name: Hāpuku
description: A heavy grey fish with a large head and a lower jaw projecting beyond the upper one.
funFact: Hāpuku have been bred through a complete life cycle in New Zealand aquaculture tanks.
clue: Deep rocky ground and offshore pinnacles.
aliases: Hapuka, Hapuku, Groper, Grouper, Bass groper (for bass), Wreckfish, puka, Hāpuka, Whāpuku, Kawerei, Moeone (bass), Ngutoro (bass)

name: Butterfish
description: A slim kelp-dweller whose long dorsal and anal fins run along a brown, green or dark blue body.
funFact: Butterfish are unusual among reef fish because seaweed makes up almost their entire diet.
clue: Kelp beds and shallow rocky coasts.
aliases: Greenbone, Greenbone butterfish, Kelp fish, butter fish, Mararī, Rarī, Marare, Matohe, Tarao, Kōeaea

name: Rig
description: A slender coastal shark with small pale spots on a bronze-grey back and no dorsal fin spines.
funFact: Rig are endemic: their natural range is confined to New Zealand.
clue: Harbours, shallow bays and sandy or muddy seabeds.
aliases: Rig shark, Lemonfish, Spotted dogfish, Smoothhound, Spotted smoothhound, Gummy shark, lemon fish, Pioke (also used for spiny dogfish), Makō, Mangō (also a general word for shark), Pīokeoke

name: Yellowbelly flounder
description: An oval flatfish with both eyes on the upper right side and a distinctive yellow underside.
funFact: It is the predominant flounder in many northern estuaries.
clue: Sheltered muddy harbours, estuaries and tidal flats.
aliases: Yellow-belly flounder, Flounder, Pātiki-tōtara, Pātiki (all flounders)
imageCredit: Image: Lisa Bennett, iNaturalist · CC BY

name: Red cod
description: A pinkish-brown cod with a small barbel beneath its chin. The dark patch at the base of the pectoral fin helps distinguish it.
clue: Sandy and muddy bottoms, especially in cooler coastal waters.
funFact: A small chin barbel and dark pectoral-fin base help distinguish red cod.
imageCredit: Original AI illustration; retained FINDEX species.

name: Jack mackerel
description: A small silver schooling fish with a blue-green back and firm scutes along its sides.
funFact: Three jack mackerel species occur in New Zealand waters.
clue: Harbours and coastal schools; often encountered from wharves.
aliases: Pacific jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), Chilean jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), jurel, jack mackeral, jack macks, yellowtail

name: Albacore tuna
description: A compact blue and silver tuna with exceptionally long pectoral fins reaching back along its body.
funFact: Fish visiting New Zealand belong to a stock spread across the South Pacific.
clue: Summer offshore waters, from northern coasts to the South Island west coast.
aliases: Albacore tuna, longfin tuna, albie

name: Blue warehou
description: A silvery fish with a darker blue-grey back and a small head. It can form schools in coastal waters.
clue: Coastal waters and continental shelf edges.
funFact: Blue warehou can gather in schools over the continental shelf.
imageCredit: Original AI illustration; retained FINDEX species.

name: Trumpeter
description: A golden-brown reef fish with three dark lengthwise stripes and thick lips.
funFact: Its extended early life near the surface helps disperse young fish widely.
clue: Cooler southern reefs, Stewart Island and the Chatham Rise.
aliases: Striped trumpeter, Kohikohi, Koekohe

name: Sand Flounder
description: A diamond-shaped flatfish with both eyes on its right side and a pale underside.
funFact: Its upper-side colouring can shift to blend with the seabed.
clue: Sand and mud in bays, estuaries and coastal shallows.
aliases: Flounder, Pātiki

name: Hoki
description: A long silver fish whose body narrows into a pointed tail without a separate tail fin.
funFact: Female hoki generally grow larger than males.
clue: Shelf slopes around New Zealand, commonly 200–600 m deep.
aliases: Blue grenadier, whiptail, blue hake

name: Pōrae
description: A deep blue-silver reef fish easily recognised by its conspicuously thick lips.
funFact: Pōrae can live for at least three decades.
clue: Northern rocky coasts from Northland to the Bay of Plenty.
aliases: Grey morwong, Blue morwong, Rubberlip morwong, Big lips

name: Stargazer
description: A broad-headed seabed ambusher with upward-facing eyes set on top of its bony head.
funFact: This giant stargazer occurs naturally only around New Zealand.
clue: Soft seabeds, especially around the South Island and Chatham Rise.
aliases: Monkfish, Giant stargazer, bulldog, Pūwhara, Kourepoua, Moamoa

name: Golden Snapper
description: An orange-red fish with oversized eyes and a deeply forked red tail.
funFact: Its common name is misleading: it belongs to a different family from snapper.
clue: Deeper coastal reefs, mainly in northern New Zealand.
aliases: Red snapper, Redfish, Nannygai, Eastern nannygai, King snapper, Koarea

name: Leatherjacket
description: An oval reef fish with a small mouth, leathery skin and a prominent spine above the eye.
funFact: Rough and smooth forms once considered separate species are now grouped together.
clue: Coastal reefs and weed beds around much of New Zealand.
aliases: Creamfish, smooth leatherjacket, velvet leatherjacket, leather jacket, Kōkiri

name: Pacific Bluefin Tuna
description: A very large tuna with short pectoral fins, a dark back and dark keels beside its tail.
funFact: These visitors travel here from spawning grounds in the North Pacific.
clue: Offshore waters; large winter visitors occur off the South Island west coast.
aliases: Northern bluefin tuna, bluefin, blue fin tuna

name: Orange Roughy
description: A brick-red deep-sea fish with a dark mouth and hard scales along its belly.
funFact: Orange roughy may live beyond a century and take decades to mature.
clue: Deep slopes and rises, commonly 750–1,200 m down.
aliases: Slimehead, roughy, Nihorota

name: Barracouta
description: A long steely-blue fish with prominent teeth and a dark patch on the first dorsal fin.
funFact: Barracouta grow quickly and usually live for fewer than ten years.
clue: Coastal schools, particularly around the South Island.
aliases: Snoek, couta, Mangā

name: Gemfish
description: A long silver fish with a bluish back and a lateral line that splits into two branches.
funFact: Its forked lateral line is a useful way to distinguish it from barracouta.
clue: Continental shelf and upper-slope waters.
aliases: Silver gemfish, silver kingfish, southern kingfish, gem fish, Tīkati, Makataharaki, Mātataharaki

name: Bluenose
description: A sturdy blue-grey fish with a blunt face and large blue eyes edged in gold.
funFact: Ageing studies indicate that bluenose can live for more than 40 years.
clue: Deep offshore reefs, seamounts and drop-offs.
aliases: Bluenose warehou, blue-eye trevalla, deep-sea trevalla, Antarctic butterfish, bonita, Griffin's silverfish, stone eye, blue nose, Matiri

name: Black Oreo
description: A dark, deep-bodied fish with large eyes and a small upward-pointing mouth.
funFact: Black oreo are thought to be capable of living beyond 100 years.
clue: Deep southern slopes, including the Chatham Rise and Campbell Plateau.
aliases: Black oreo dory, black dory

name: Yellowfin Tuna
description: A warm-water tuna whose yellow fins and finlets stand out against metallic blue and silver sides.
funFact: Swimming with an open mouth keeps water moving across its gills.
clue: Northern offshore waters during summer.
aliases: Yellowfin, ahi, yellow fin tuna

name: Yellow-eyed Mullet
description: A small silver fish with a bright yellow eye, often seen schooling around wharves.
funFact: Often nicknamed herring locally, it actually belongs to the mullet family.
clue: Harbours, river mouths and sandy beaches.
aliases: Yelloweye mullet, herring, Aua, Makawhiti, Kātaha, Kātaka, Mokohiti

name: Ling
description: An elongated pink-orange fish with pale mottling and slender, feeler-like pelvic fins.
funFact: Female ling typically grow faster and larger than males.
clue: Deep continental shelf and slope waters, especially in the south.
aliases: Kingklip, pink ling, pink cusk-eel, ling cod, Hokarari, Hoka, Rari

name: Chinook Salmon
description: A large introduced salmon with black gums along its lower jaw; also called king or quinnat salmon.
funFact: Chinook are the largest salmon or trout found in New Zealand.
clue: South Island east-coast rivers and coastal waters during migrations.
aliases: King salmon, quinnat salmon, Hāmana

name: Brown Trout
description: An introduced trout with spotted brown or silver flanks and a tail that usually has few spots.
funFact: New Zealand brown trout descend from introductions made in the late 1860s.
clue: Rivers and lakes throughout much of New Zealand.
aliases: Brownie, sea-run trout, Tarauta, Taraute

name: Grey Mullet
description: A robust silver schooling fish with a blunt head and a thick fleshy covering over much of the eye.
funFact: Large females can release around a million eggs during spawning.
clue: Shallow northern harbours, mangroves and estuaries.
aliases: Mullet, flathead mullet, sea mullet, striped mullet, Kanae, Hopuhopu, Kanae raukura

name: Hake
description: A slender deepwater fish with a projecting lower jaw that leaves some teeth visible.
funFact: Female hake can outgrow males, reaching more than a metre long.
clue: Southern slopes, the Chatham Rise and Campbell Plateau.
aliases: Southern hake, whiting, Tīkati, Kehe

name: Sole
description: An oval flatfish widest near its rounded head, rather than the diamond outline of a sand flounder.
funFact: New Zealand sole is endemic to this country's waters.
clue: Shallow sandy seabeds, especially around the South Island.
aliases: New Zealand sole, common sole, Pātiki rore, Pātiki rori, Horihori, Raututu, Tarore, Pakeke

name: Whitebait
scientific: Galaxias maculatus, Galaxias brevipinnis, Galaxias fasciatus, Galaxias argenteus, Galaxias postvectis
description: Whitebait are translucent juveniles of five native galaxiid species; most of the catch consists of young īnanga.
funFact: Protecting streamside plants helps preserve the places where īnanga lay their eggs.
clue: Coastal streams, wetlands and river mouths during upstream migration.
aliases: Īnanga, Inanga, White bait, Īnanga (the fish and its whitebait)
imageCredit: Whitebait (juvenile īnanga). Image: Greg Wallis, iNaturalist, flipped · CC BY 4.0 · Whitebait, as caught. Image: Stewart Nimmo, Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Adult īnanga, which whitebait grow into. Image: Te Papa (P.005625), background removed · CC BY 4.0

name: School Shark
description: A slim grey shark with a pointed snout, no spots and a conspicuous upper tail lobe.
funFact: Unlike rig and spiny dogfish, its back has neither pale spots nor dorsal fin spines.
clue: Coastal waters in summer and deeper offshore water in winter.
aliases: Tope, Grey shark, Tope shark, Kapetā, Tupere, Makohuarau (Also recorded for spiny dogfish.)
imageCredit: Image: nick_goldwater, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Image: AshlieJMcivor, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Spiny Dogfish
description: A small brown-grey shark with scattered pale spots and a spine ahead of each dorsal fin.
funFact: The paired dorsal spines help separate it from rig and school shark.
clue: Coastal and shelf waters, especially around the South Island.
aliases: Spotted spiny dogfish, Piked dogfish, Spineback, Pioke (also used for rig), Kāraerae, Koinga, Mangō hapū, Mangō pekepeke, Makohuarau (Also recorded for school shark.)
imageCredit: Image: Lorraine Cook, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Image: Magnefl, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Carpet Shark
description: A stocky, blotched catshark with a broad head and two dorsal fins positioned far back.
funFact: It can inflate its belly with water or air when disturbed.
clue: Rocky reefs and adjacent sand around New Zealand.
aliases: Draughtsboard shark, New Zealand carpet shark, Carpetshark, Pekapeka
imageCredit: Image: Arnim Littek, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Image: Py1jtp, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY-SA 3.0

name: Bronze Whaler
description: A large bronze-backed shark with a pale belly and a broad rounded snout.
funFact: Bronze whalers are regular warm-season visitors to northern coastal waters.
clue: Northern bays, harbours and open coastal waters.
aliases: Bronze shark, Bronze whaler shark, Copper shark, bronzie, Horopekapeka, Tōiki, Ngengero (Te Aka also gives ngengero for the blue shark), Matawhā, Ngerungeru
imageCredit: Image: Tia Offner, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Image: Oscar Dove, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

name: Mako Shark
description: A streamlined shark with a pointed snout, blue back, pale underside and long visible teeth.
funFact: Its sharp, conical teeth remain visible even when its mouth is closed.
clue: Offshore waters around New Zealand.
aliases: Shortfin mako, Mako, Blue pointer, Mackerel shark, Mako (means the shark or a shark tooth; the name has been adopted worldwide), Ngutukao
imageCredit: Image: Hugues Evano (IFREMER), Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Image: Arnim Littek, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

creditLinks.text: Hugues Evano (IFREMER), Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Hammerhead Shark
description: A grey shark with a broad hammer-shaped head and tall first dorsal fin.
funFact: The smooth hammerhead is the hammerhead species recorded in New Zealand.
clue: Northern coastal waters, with young fish in shallow bays.
aliases: Smooth hammerhead, Smooth hammerhead shark, Hammerhead, Mangōpare (also the name of a kōwhaiwhai pattern that symbolises the hammerhead), Kakere
imageCredit: Image: Jonathan Couch and A. F. Lydon, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · Public domain · Image: Robert Briggs, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY-SA 4.0

creditLinks.text: Jonathan Couch and A. F. Lydon, Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Great White Shark
description: A powerful grey-backed shark with a white belly, conical snout and triangular serrated teeth.
funFact: Great whites belong to the same shark order as makos and basking sharks.
clue: Coastal and offshore waters around New Zealand.
aliases: White pointer, White pointer shark, White shark, Mangō taniwha, Mangō ururoa, Tupa (Ngāi Tahu name)
imageCredit: Image: Elias Levy, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY 2.0 · Image: Robin White, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

creditLinks.text: Elias Levy, Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Stingrays
description: Short-tail and long-tail stingrays have broad discs with rounded wings and a slender tail.
funFact: Their rounded wings ripple as they move; eagle rays have pointed wings that flap.
clue: Bays, estuaries and sandy coastal bottoms.
aliases: Short-tail stingray, Short-tailed stingray, Long-tail stingray, Long-tailed stingray, Whiptail stingray, Whai (rays and skates in general), Roha (short-tail stingray), Pākaurua (short-tail stingray), Whai repo (also the eagle ray)
imageCredit: Short-tail stingray. Image: Peter Crowcroft, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Long-tail stingray. Image: Shaun Lee, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

name: Eagle Ray
description: A ray with pointed wings, a projecting head and a long whip-like tail.
funFact: Its wing strokes resemble a bird's flight, giving the eagle ray its name.
clue: Shallow harbours, estuaries and coastal bays.
aliases: Whai keo, Whai repo (also used for the short-tail and long-tail stingrays)
imageCredit: Image: Lachlan Macnaughtan, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Image: Andy McKay, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

creditLinks.text: Lachlan Macnaughtan, Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Basking Shark
description: A huge shark with a cavernous mouth and long gill slits, feeding by filtering tiny animals.
funFact: This plankton eater is the world's second-largest fish.
clue: Cool coastal and offshore waters; uncommon in New Zealand.
aliases: Mangō reremai, Reremai
imageCredit: Image: Green Fire Productions, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY 2.0 · Image: Devon Bradley, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

creditLinks.text: Green Fire Productions, Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Whale Shark
description: A broad-headed giant with pale spots and stripes arranged across its dark back.
funFact: The world's largest fish feeds on small prey filtered from the water.
clue: Occasional summer visits to northern New Zealand.
imageCredit: Image: FGBNMS/Eckert, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · Public domain · Image: Holmbergius, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY 3.0

name: Manta Ray
description: Oceanic mantas and smaller devil rays have broad pointed wings and paired head fins.
funFact: Head fins help funnel plankton-rich water towards the mouth.
clue: Northern open waters in spring and summer.
aliases: Oceanic manta ray, Giant manta ray, Giant oceanic manta ray, Spinetail devil ray, Spine-tailed devil ray, Giant devil ray, Japanese devil ray, Devil ray, Devilfish, Te Whai Rahi (oceanic manta ray)
imageCredit: Oceanic manta ray. Image: Georgina Jones, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Spinetail devil ray. Image: Julien Renoult, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

name: Pāua
description: A black-footed sea snail with an ear-shaped shell and a row of breathing holes.
funFact: Its bluish blood uses copper to carry oxygen.
clue: Shallow rocky shores and surge-washed reefs.
aliases: Blackfoot pāua, Ordinary pāua, Abalone, Tuke o rangi, Kararuri (young pāua)
imageCredit: Image: Javier, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Image: Michael Berardozzi, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Image: Saryu Mae 前 朝琉, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

creditLinks.text: Saryu Mae 前 朝琉, iNaturalist, background removed

name: Crayfish
description: A reddish spiny rock lobster with long antennae and a segmented tail, lacking large pincer claws.
funFact: Its transparent larvae may spend one to two years drifting offshore.
clue: Rocky reefs and crevices around the coast.
aliases: Rock lobster, Spiny rock lobster, Red rock lobster, Southern rock lobster, cray, Kōura, Kōura papatea, Kōura matapara
imageCredit: Image: Michael Berardozzi, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Image: Michael Berardozzi, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

name: Kina
description: A round green-brown sea urchin covered in movable spines, grazing on reef seaweed.
funFact: Its mouth contains a five-toothed structure known as Aristotle's lantern.
clue: Shallow rocky reefs and kelp forests.
aliases: Sea urchin, Sea egg, New Zealand sea urchin, Pūrau, Ateate (kina roe)
imageCredit: Image: Tony Wills, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY-SA 4.0

name: Pipi
description: A smooth oval clam found in clean sand near tidal harbour mouths.
funFact: Young pipi drift as larvae for several weeks before settling into sand.
clue: Sandy tidal banks with strong currents.
imageCredit: Image: Shaun Thompson, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY 4.0

creditLinks.text: Shaun Thompson, Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Oysters
scientific: Ostrea chilensis, Saccostrea glomerata, Magallana gigas
description: This entry covers Pacific, native rock and Bluff oysters; their shells and habitats differ.
funFact: Bluff oysters brood their larvae inside their shells before releasing them.
clue: Northern intertidal rocks and deeper southern oyster beds.
aliases: Bluff oyster, Dredge oyster, Flat oyster, Rock oyster, Pacific oyster, Tio (rock oyster), Tio para (Bluff (dredge) oyster)
imageCredit: Pacific oyster. Image: Tony Wills, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Dredge (Bluff) oyster. Image: Auckland Museum, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY 4.0

creditLinks.text: Auckland Museum, Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Scallops
description: A ribbed fan-shaped shellfish with a flat upper shell and a more curved lower one.
funFact: Each New Zealand scallop can produce both eggs and sperm.
clue: Sandy or silty seabeds, often partly recessed in the sediment.
aliases: New Zealand scallop, Tipa (also pure or tupa), Kuakua
imageCredit: Image: Jacqui Geux, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0 · Image: Auckland Museum, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY 4.0

creditLinks.text: Auckland Museum, Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Tuatua
description: A smooth triangular surf clam with an angled hinge, found on exposed sandy beaches.
funFact: Tuatua can reach roughly 40–70 mm in about three years.
clue: Clean sand on open ocean surf beaches.
aliases: Surf clam
imageCredit: Image: Saryu Mae 前 朝琉, iNaturalist, background removed · CC BY 4.0

creditLinks.text: Saryu Mae 前 朝琉, iNaturalist, background removed

name: Cockles
description: A rounded, ribbed shellfish living just beneath sheltered tidal sand and mud.
funFact: Some New Zealand cockles can live for around 25 years.
clue: Sheltered harbour sandflats and mudflats.
aliases: New Zealand cockle, Tuangi (also hūwai, tuaki or huangi depending on iwi dialect (NIWA))
imageCredit: Image: GrahamBould, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · Public domain

name: Mussels
description: Green-lipped mussels have a green shell edge; smaller blue mussels have blue-black shells.
funFact: Tough byssus threads anchor mussel clusters to rocks and piles.
clue: Rocky shores, wharf piles and coastal mussel beds.
aliases: Green-lipped mussel, Greenshell mussel, Blue mussel, Kuku (green-lipped mussel, Perna canaliculus), Kūtai (mussel of several species)
imageCredit: Image: Richard Giddins from London, UK, Wikimedia Commons, background removed · CC BY 2.0

creditLinks.text: Richard Giddins from London, UK, Wikimedia Commons, background removed

name: Arrow squid
description: An elongated squid with large eyes, a pointed mantle and triangular rear fins.
funFact: Arrow squid have eight arms plus two longer feeding tentacles.
clue: Coastal and offshore waters around New Zealand.
aliases: Squid, calamari
imageCredit: Original AI sprite generated from an anatomical description; FINDEX artwork used as a style reference.

name: Common octopus
description: A mottled reddish-brown octopus with eight muscular arms and rows of suckers.
funFact: Small common octopuses can be found sheltering in tidal rock pools.
clue: Rocky reefs, crevices and coastal seabeds.
aliases: Octopus, wheke, Macroctopus maorum, Octopus maorum
imageCredit: Original AI sprite generated from an anatomical description; FINDEX artwork used as a style reference.

name: Mahi-mahi
description: A brilliantly coloured fish with golden sides, a blue dorsal fin and a blunt forehead.
funFact: Males develop a much steeper forehead than females.
clue: Warm offshore waters; occasional summer visitors to northern New Zealand.
aliases: Mahi mahi, mahimahi, dolphinfish, dorado
imageCredit: Original AI sprite generated from an anatomical description; FINDEX artwork used as a style reference.

name: Rainbow trout
description: A silver and olive trout with a pink side stripe and dark spots across its body and tail.
funFact: New Zealand rainbows descend from fish introduced from North America.
clue: Freshwater lakes and rivers, including central North Island fisheries.
imageCredit: Original AI sprite generated from an anatomical description; FINDEX artwork used as a style reference.

name: Parore
description: A deep-bodied grey-green fish with dark vertical bars and a small mouth.
funFact: Parore are also known as luderick.
clue: Northern estuaries, weed beds and shallow rocky coasts.
imageCredit: Original AI sprite generated from an anatomical description; FINDEX artwork used as a style reference.

name: Skipjack tuna
description: A compact tuna with a dark back and several dark stripes along its silver lower flanks.
funFact: Skipjack travel far beyond New Zealand as part of their oceanic migrations.
clue: Northern open waters, often in fast-moving surface schools.
imageCredit: Original AI sprite generated from an anatomical description; FINDEX artwork used as a style reference.

name: Striped marlin
description: A streamlined billfish with a spear-like snout, tall dorsal fin and blue vertical flank bars.
funFact: Striped marlin are the most abundant marlin in New Zealand's gamefish fishery.
clue: Northern offshore waters, particularly in summer and autumn.
imageCredit: Original AI sprite generated from an anatomical description; FINDEX artwork used as a style reference.

name: Swordfish
description: A powerful billfish with a long flattened bill, dark back and crescent-shaped tail.
funFact: Swordfish occur in New Zealand waters throughout the year.
clue: Offshore waters, including deep daytime habitat.
aliases: Broadbill
imageCredit: Original AI sprite generated from an anatomical description; FINDEX artwork used as a style reference.

name: Blue mackerel
description: A streamlined silver fish with a blue-green back patterned in dark wavy stripes.
funFact: Blue mackerel schools are among those recorded by New Zealand's aerial fish-spotting surveys.
clue: Coastal and open-water schools around New Zealand.
imageCredit: Original AI sprite generated from an anatomical description; FINDEX artwork used as a style reference.

name: Spotty
description: A small mottled wrasse with thick lips and a dark patch on its side.
